plan.contextChunk: This figure contains six panels (a)–(f) illustrating the operation of insertion sort on an array of six integers. Each panel shows a horizontal array of six cells indexed 1 through 6 above the cells. Gray cells to the left of the current key represent the already-sorted subarray; the current key is shown in a black cell with white text; white cells to the right remain unsorted. Curved arrows below the array indicate element movements: a bold black arrow points to the slot where the key will be inserted, while lighter gray arrows indicate elements shifting one position to the right to make room. Panel (a) shows the initial array [5, 2, 4, 6, 1, 3] with key 2 at position 2 moving left past 5. Panel (b) shows key 4 at position 3 being inserted into sorted subarray [2, 5]. Panel (c) shows key 6 at position 4 requiring no movement as it is already the largest element in the sorted prefix. Panel (d) shows key 1 at position 5 shifting four elements rightward to reach position 1. Panel (e) shows key 3 at position 6 shifting three elements rightward to reach its correct position. Panel (f) shows the final sorted array [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] with no black cell and no arrows. This figure illustrates the insertion sort algorithm step by step, demonstrating how each key is extracted and inserted into its correct position within the growing sorted subarray to its left.

interactionPlan.concept: Insertion sort grows a sorted prefix one element at a time by extracting each new key, comparing it leftward against the sorted prefix, and shifting larger elements right until the key's correct position is found.

white cells representing the unsorted remainder (right of the key)

interactions.label: Implement insertion sort

api.does: extracts A[j] as the current key — marks that cell black; returns the key value
returns true if A[i] > current key
copies A[i] into A[i+1] — shifts one element right to make room; the ONLY way to move existing elements
places the current key into A[i] — marks positions 1..i as sorted (gray)
adds a text annotation below the array for your own commentary

interactions.frame: the whole 6-cell array with index labels above, the current key cell in black, sorted prefix in gray, unsorted cells in white, and curved arrows below showing the most recent shift or insert operation
interactions.success_check: Array is sorted in non-decreasing order: A[1] <= A[2] <= A[3] <= A[4] <= A[5] <= A[6]
interactions.teaches: The inner while-loop is the heart of insertion sort: it walks leftward through the sorted prefix, shifting each element that is larger than the key one position right, until it finds the gap where the key belongs — the number of shifts equals the number of inversions the key has with the sorted prefix

interactions.label: Reveal reference solution
interactions.teaches: Comparing your implementation against the reference reveals whether your loop bounds and shift logic match the standard CLRS formulation

demo_steps.title: The goal: grow a sorted prefix
demo_steps.narration: The array starts as [5, 2, 4, 6, 1, 3]. Insertion sort processes elements left to right: after processing position j, positions 1 through j are sorted. Watch how each key is extracted (black cell) and inserted into the gray sorted prefix.

demo_steps.title: Trace one iteration: key = 2
demo_steps.narration: For j=2, the key is 2. compare_with_key(1) asks: is A[1]=5 > 2? Yes — so shift(1) copies 5 rightward to position 2. Now i=0, the loop ends, and insert(1) places 2 at position 1. The sorted prefix is now [2, 5].

demo_steps.title: Your turn: write the full algorithm
demo_steps.narration: Now implement the complete insertion sort using the five operations. The outer loop visits j = 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. For each j, extract the key, shift larger elements right, then insert. If your final array isn't sorted, check your while-loop condition — an off-by-one on the lower bound is the most common bug.

demo_steps.title: Compare with the reference
demo_steps.narration: Reveal the reference solution and compare it line-by-line with yours. Notice how get_key, the while-loop with compare_with_key, shift, and insert correspond exactly to the visual operations in panels (a) through (f).

interactionPlan.keyInsight: Each iteration of insertion sort resolves exactly the inversions between the new key and the sorted prefix — the number of shift operations in one pass equals the number of elements in the prefix that are larger than the key, which is why worst-case (reverse-sorted) input costs O(n²) shifts total.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Six cells in a horizontal row, each ~60px wide with a thin black border. Index numbers (1–6) centered above each cell in a serif font. Cell fill colors: gray (#C0C0C0) for sorted prefix, black (#000) with white bold text for the current key, white for unsorted. Curved arrows below the array: a bold black arrow (stroke-width 2) arcs from the key's original position to its insertion slot; thinner gray arrows (stroke-width 1.5, color #888) arc from each shifted element's old position to its new position one cell right. Panel labels (a)–(f) in bold serif to the left of each array. The final panel (f) has all cells white with no arrows. Layout: panels arranged in a 3×2 grid (a, b, c on top; d, e, f on bottom) with generous spacing. The code editor sits below or beside the array visualization, and the array redraws frame-by-frame as the learner's code executes.

discrepancies: Shift arrows are drawn as separate nested quadratic arcs (one per shift) rather than the source's single sweeping arc carrying multiple gray arrowheads, making panels (d) and (e) look busier and stylistically different from the original.

The six panels are compressed into roughly the left half of the layout beside a large code-editor workbench, so the cells, index numbers, and value labels render much smaller than in the full-width source figure.

During a live run only the panel-(a) slot is replaced by the live trace while (b)-(f) stay frozen, so the source's (a)-(f) snapshot-sequence teaching device is not dynamically reproduced across all six panels.
evaluation.notes: The static (a)-(f) reconstruction is faithful in cell colors, values, indices, gray sorted-prefix/black-key states, and the (c) self-loop, and the worker-based code-editor + playback workbench is a deep, concept-correct interaction set; the main weaknesses are the shrunken panel/label scale, the nested-arc arrow styling that departs from the source, and the live trace updating only one panel.
action_items: Give the 2x3 panel grid more of the viewport (or raise CW/CH and the index/value font sizes) so the six panels and their labels are comfortably legible at inline size, matching the source's visual prominence.

Draw each panel's shifts as one continuous sweeping arc with several gray arrowheads (and the black insert arc beneath it) to match the source's arrow style instead of emitting one nested quadratic curve per shift.
Extend the live run to advance through all six panel slots as a sequence (or add a panel/step selector) so the dynamic trace mirrors the (a)-(f) progression rather than overwriting only panel (a).
